## Balanced Sample Sizes

In the examples we've been dealing with so far, our factorial ANOVAs have had **balanced** sample sizes

- Sample $n$ in every cell


```{r}
dat <- read.csv("../../data/wine east west.csv")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
table(dat$hill, dat$condition)
```


This is desirable when possible

- Maximizes statistical power
- Makes factors **orthogonal**
    - There aren't **more** or **less** cases in a given condition for the east rather than west side of the hill
    
Not always possible!


## Another Example


::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

**Original Study**:

Exline, J. J., Baumeister, R. F., Zell, A. L., Kraft, A., & Witvliet, C. V. O. (2008). Not so innocent: Does seeing one's own capacity for wrongdoing predict forgiveness? *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, *94*, 495-515.

**Replication study link**: [https://osf.io/nrjs5](https://osf.io/nrjs5)

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}



**Steps**:

* Recall a time you were hurt, offended, harmed
* Complete a vengefulness questionnaire
* Answer questions about personal capability and empathy, examples: 
    + "Given the right circumstances, do you think that you could be capable of doing something just as bad?"
    + "Thinking back over your entire life, do you think that you have ever done anything as bad as what the other person did?"
    
**DV**: Vengefulness scores

**IV1**: Order of conditions (capability/empathy first, vengefulness first)

**IV2**: Gender (male/female)

::: 

## Interaction Plot

```{r}
#| include: false

library(forcats)
library(ez)

dat <- read_csv("../../data/Exline data.csv")
dat <- dat %>% mutate(sex = as_factor(sex..),
                      condition = as_factor(condition),
                      condition = recode(condition,
                                         "1" = "capability first" ,
                                         "2" = "vengefulness first" ),
                       gender = recode(sex, "1" = "male", "2" = "female"))


```

```{r}
#| message: false


lm1 <- lm(vengefulness ~ condition * gender, dat)
library(ggeffects)
ggp1 <- ggpredict(lm1, terms = c("condition","gender"))
plot(ggp1) + ylim(c(0, 5)) + labs(color = "gender", title = NULL)

```


## Unequal Sample Sizes

In this dataset, not all groups have equal sample sizes:

```{r}
exline <- dat
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

table(exline$gender, exline$condition)
```

**The research design problem**:

- Missing data (dropout, unusable responses)
- Pre-existing groups may be hard to sample in equal proportions

## The Statistical Problem

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

- If sample sizes in ANOVA are unequal, then effects are **correlated**
- For male, $n_{\text{capability first}} > n_{\text{vengefulness first}}$
- For female, $n_{\text{capability first}} < n_{\text{vengefulness first}}$

Why might this be a problem?

- [How will this affect the **marginal** effect of gender?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [Will the condition order maybe have an unintended impact on the marginal means of gender?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [Because there are more males who saw capability first, the marginal mean of male is going to be weighted more towards capability first]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [Because there are more females who saw vengefulness first, the marginal mean of female is going to be weighted more towards vengefulness first]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
        - [Effects of gender and condition are **confounded**]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

:::

## Different Example

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

Number of errors made in a driving simulation

| | **Non-Drinking** | **Drinking** | **Row Means** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Michigan** | 13 15 16 12<br><br>$\bar{y}_{11} = 14$ | 18 20 22 19 21<br>23 17 18 22 20<br>$\bar{y}_{12} = 20$ | <br><br>$\bar{y}_{1\bullet} = 18.29$ |
| **Arizona** | 9 11 14 10 6<br>8 12 13 11 6<br>$\bar{y}_{21} = 10$ | 28 29 21 20 22<br><br>$\bar{y}_{22} = 24$ | <br><br>$\bar{y}_{2\bullet} = 14.67$ |
| **Col Means** | $\bar{y}_{\bullet 1} = 11.14$ | $\bar{y}_{\bullet 2} = 21.33$ | |

What do you think about these results?

- Are there effects of drinking?
- Are there differences by state?
- How might the **marginal** means differ if we had equal sample sizes?

:::


## Equalizing $n$'s

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

| | **Non-Drinking** | **Drinking** | **Row Means** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Michigan** | 17 13 15 16 12<br>11 13 15 16 12<br>$\bar{y}_{11} = 14$ | 18 20 22 19 21<br>23 17 18 22 20<br>$\bar{y}_{12} = 20$ | <br>$\bar{y}_{1\bullet} = 17.00$ |
| **Arizona** | 9 11 14 10 6<br>8 12 13 11 6<br>$\bar{y}_{21} = 10$ | 28 29 21 20 22<br>20 28 24 21 27<br>$\bar{y}_{22} = 24$ |<br>$\bar{y}_{2\bullet} = 17.00$ |
| **Col Means** | $\bar{y}_{\bullet 1} = 12.00$ | $\bar{y}_{\bullet 2} = 22.00$ | |

If we equalized the sample sizes while holding the cell means constant:

- Still a clear effect of drinking, no longer an effect of state!
- The effect of state was really because we had more drinkers in Michigan and more non-drinkers in Arizona
- If we have the same number of drinkers in each state, it becomes obvious drinking differentiated errors, not geographic location
:::



## Equal Sample Sizes

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

If sample sizes are **equal**, then group membership is **uncorrelated**

- 1 = level 1, 2 = level 2
- $N = 2$ in each cell

| **Factor 1** | **Factor 2** |
|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | 1 |
| 1 | <span style="color: red;">1</span> |
| 1 | 2 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 2 |

$\text{cor}(\text{Factor 1}, \text{Factor 2}) = 0$

:::

## Unequal Sample Sizes


::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

If sample sizes are **unequal**, then group membership is **correlated**

- 1 = level 1, 2 = level 2
- $N =$ 1, 2, or 3 in each cell

| **Factor 1** | **Factor 2** |
|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | 1 |
| 1 | <span style="color: red;">2</span> |
| 1 | 2 |
| 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 2 |

$\text{cor}(\text{Factor 1}, \text{Factor 2}) = -0.26$

:::




## Balanced Sums of Squares

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5

library(ggplot2)
library(ggforce)

circles <- data.frame(
  x = c(-1.8, 1.8, 0),
  y = c(1.2, 1.2, -1.2),
  r = c(1.3, 1.3, 1.3),
  label = c("SSA", "SSB", "SSAB"),
  color = c("#3b82f6", "#ef4444", "#eab308")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = -4, xmax = 4, ymin = -3.2, ymax = 3.2), fill = "#e2e8f0", color = "gray70") +
  geom_circle(data = circles, aes(x0 = x, y0 = y, r = r, fill = color), color = "gray30", alpha = 0.85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_text(data = circles, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), fontface = "bold", size = 6, color = "white") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.8, y = -2.2, label = "SSW", fontface = "bold", size = 7, color = "#334155") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void()
```



## Unbalanced SS

If sample sizes are **unequal**, group membership is correlated.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5


# Define circle centers and radii
circles <- data.frame(
  x0 = c(-1.25, 1.25, 0),
  y0 = c(1.25, 1.25, -1.25),
  r = c(2, 2, 2),
  color = c("#3b82f6", "#ef4444", "#eab308")
)

# Label coordinates for regions 1 to 7
regions <- data.frame(
  x = c(-1.5, 1.5, 0, -0.75, 0.75, 0, 0),
  y = c(1.5, 1.5, -1.5, 0, 0, 0.25, 1.5),
  label = as.character(1:7)
)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = -4, xmax = 4, ymin = -4, ymax = 4), fill = "#e2e8f0", color = "gray70") +
  geom_circle(data = circles, aes(x0 = x0, y0 = y0, r = r, fill = color), alpha = 0.4, color = "gray30", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  geom_text(data = regions, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label), fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
  annotate("text", x = -2.5, y = 2.8, label = "SSA", fontface = "bold", size = 7, color = "#1d4ed8") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 2.8, label = "SSB", fontface = "bold", size = 7, color = "#b91c1c") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = -2.8, label = "SSAB", fontface = "bold", size = 7, color = "#a16207") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = -3.2, label = "SSW", fontface = "bold", size = 6, color = "#334155") +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

library(ez)
library(car)
data(npk)
npk$id <- 1:24

d <- npk[-1, ] # Create unbalanced dataset

type1  <- ezANOVA(d, dv = yield, wid = factor(id), between = .(N, P), type = 1)
type1b <- ezANOVA(d, dv = yield, wid = factor(id), between = .(P, N), type = 1)
type2  <- ezANOVA(d, dv = yield, wid = factor(id), between = .(N, P), type = 2)
type3  <- ezANOVA(d, dv = yield, wid = factor(id), between = .(N, P), type = 3)
```

## Type III SS 


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5

# Function to draw highlighting diagrams
draw_ss_diagram <- function(highlight_regions) {
  circles <- data.frame(
    x0 = c(-1.25, 1.25, 0),
    y0 = c(1.25, 1.25, -1.25),
    r = c(2, 2, 2),
    color = c("#3b82f6", "#ef4444", "#eab308")
  )
  
  regions <- data.frame(
    x = c(-1.5, 1.5, 0, -0.75, 0.75, 0, 0),
    y = c(1.5, 1.5, -1.5, 0, 0, 0.25, 1.5),
    label = as.character(1:7)
  )
  
  regions$highlight <- regions$label %in% highlight_regions
  
  ggplot() +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = -4, xmax = 4, ymin = -4, ymax = 4), fill = "#f8fafc", color = "gray80") +
    geom_circle(data = circles, aes(x0 = x0, y0 = y0, r = r, fill = color), alpha = 0.25, color = "gray50", show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_identity() +
    geom_label(data = regions, aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, fill = ifelse(highlight, "#fde047", "white")), 
               fontface = "bold", size = 5, show.legend = FALSE) +
    annotate("text", x = -2.5, y = 2.8, label = "SSA", fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
    annotate("text", x = 2.5, y = 2.8, label = "SSB", fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
    annotate("text", x = 1.3, y = -2.8, label = "SSAB", fontface = "bold", size = 6) +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_void()
}

draw_ss_diagram(c("1", "2", "3"))
```


## Type III Table

| Source | $df$ | $SS$ | Diagram Portion |
|:---|:---:|:---|:---:|
| **$A$** | $a-1$ | $SS(A \mid B, AB)$ | **1** |
| **$B$** | $b-1$ | $SS(B \mid A, AB)$ | **2** |
| **$AB$** | $(a-1)(b-1)$ | $SS(AB \mid A, B)$ | **3** |
| **Error** | $N-ab$ | | |
| **Total** | $N-1$ | | |


- Each effect is adjusted for all other effects
- **Preferred if interaction effect is of interest**

## Type II SS 



```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5

draw_ss_diagram(c("1", "4", "2", "5", "3"))
```

## Type II Table

| Source | $df$ | $SS$ | Diagram Portion |
|:---|:---:|:---|:---:|
| **$A$** | $a-1$ | $SS(A \mid B)$ | **1 + 4** |
| **$B$** | $b-1$ | $SS(B \mid A)$ | **2 + 5** |
| **$AB$** | $(a-1)(b-1)$ | $SS(AB \mid A, B)$ | **3** |
| **Error** | $N-ab$ | | |
| **Total** | $N-1$ | | |

- Tests for the independent contribution of each main effect
- **Preferred if main effects are of interest** (no significant interaction expected)



## Type I SS Way 1



```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5

draw_ss_diagram(c("1", "4", "6", "7", "2", "5", "3"))
```

## Type I Way 1 Table

Order of terms in model: $A \to B \to AB$

| Source | $df$ | &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$SS$&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; | Diagram Portion |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **$A$** | $a-1$ | $SS({\color{red} A})$ | **<span style="color: red;">1 + 4</span> + 6 + 7** |
| **$B$** | $b-1$ | $SS({\color{blue} B} \mid A)$ | **<span style="color: blue;">2 + 5</span>** |
| **$AB$** | $(a-1)(b-1)$ | ${SS(AB {\mid} A, B)}$ | **3** |
| **Error** | $N-ab$ | | |
| **Total** | $N-1$ | | |



## Type I Way 2 Table

Order of terms in model: $B \to A \to AB$

| Source | $df$ | &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$SS$&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; | Diagram Portion |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **$B$** | $b-1$ | $SS({\color{blue} B})$ | **<span style="color: blue;">2 + 5</span> + 6 + 7** |
| **$A$** | $a-1$ | $SS({\color{red} A} \mid B)$ | **<span style="color: red;">1 + 4</span>** |
| **$AB$** | $(a-1)(b-1)$ | ${SS(AB {\mid} A, B)}$ | **3** |
| **Error** | $N-ab$ | | |
| **Total** | $N-1$ | | |


## Similarities\\Differences

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

- The results for the interaction are **always** the same
- The types of SS are different ways of accounting for the **main effects**
- Type I includes the confounding effect for whichever factor is entered first
- Removes confounding factor for factor entered second
    - **Only** sensible if you think the **population** is **also** unbalanced **AND** care about that imbalance on the first factor in the model
- Type II assumes main effects are unconfounded by interaction
    - Most useful if you are OK assuming a negligible interaction **in the population**
    - If so, more powerful test of main effect
- Type III assumes main effects are confounded by interaction
    - Most useful if you are assuming a non-negligible interaction in the population
    - Main effect tests less powerful, but also main effects have less clear interpretation if interaction is present, so may not be an issue

::: 


## Recommendations I

When data are balanced, all three give the same results

When data are unbalanced:

- **Type I** is rarely appropriate 
    - Accounts for variables in a particular order
    - Only consider if you believe **population** is unbalanced and want to let that imblanace influence your results
      - E.g. can be appropriate in demography when groups do naturally differ in frequency
      - Never appropriate in randomized experiments
    - Default SS if using `aov()`

## Recommendations II & III

When data are balanced, all three give the same results

When data are unbalanced:


**Type II**

- More powerful than type III if you believe the interaction is negligible in the population
    - Sometimes interpreted as "interaction is non-significant"
- Default SS if using `ezANOVA`

**Type III**

- Recommended if interaction effect is non-negligible
- Default in SPSS which made this approach popular/conventional

## Types in `R`

The way `R` is programmed, Type II is straightforward. However, Type III **is not always**

- Some packages **cannot** get Type III if the model uses dummy coding as contrast
- Requires contrasts to be orthogonal
    - Sum to zero
    - Sum of products of pairs of contrast columns must sum to zero
- Dummy coding does not sum to zero, despite being default in `R` and most common contrast scheme
- Effects coding is a viable alternative


## Exline Data Coding

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

| Group / Cell | IV1: Order | IV2: Gender | Dummy $D_1$ | Dummy $D_2$ | Dummy $D_1 \times D_2$ | Effects $E_1$ | Effects $E_2$ | Effects $E_1 \times E_2$ |
|:---|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Cell 1** | Cap/Emp First | Male | 0 | 0 | 0 | -1 | -1 | +1 |
| **Cell 2** | Cap/Emp First | Female | 0 | 1 | 0 | -1 | +1 | -1 |
| **Cell 3** | Vengefulness First | Male | 1 | 0 | 0 | +1 | -1 | -1 |
| **Cell 4** | Vengefulness First | Female | 1 | 1 | 1 | +1 | +1 | +1 |

:::

- Coding schemes (columns) always sum to 0 in effects coding (orthogonality)
- Do not sum to 0 in dummy coding (non-orthogonality)

## Exline Type I

The littel-**a** `anova()` function (built into `R`) gives us Type I

```{r}
#| echo: true

a_t1 <- aov(vengefulness ~ condition * gender, dat)
anova(a_t1)

```

## Exline Type II `car`

For Type II and III we can use `car::Anova()` or `ez::ezANOVA()`. For Type II using `car::Anova()`:

```{r}
#| echo: true

library(car)
a_t2 <- aov(vengefulness ~ condition * gender, dat)
Anova(a_t2, type = 2)

```

## Exline Type II `ez`

For Type II and III we can use `car::Anova()` or `ez::ezANOVA()`. For Type II using `ez::ezANOVA()`:

```{r}
#| echo: true

library(ez)
ezANOVA(exline, dv = vengefulness, wid = ID, between = c(gender, condition), 
        type = 2)$ANOVA

```


`ezANOVA()` will always warn you about unbalanced sample sizes


## Exline Type III `car`

For Type II and III we can use `car::Anova()` or `ez::ezANOVA()`. For Type III using `car::Anova()`, we **must set orthogonal (e.g. effects coded) contrasts before using `aov()`** or the results will be incorrect. We can do this globally for all factors by first specifying `options(contrasts = c(unordered = "contr.sum", ordered = "contr.poly"))`

- `contr.sum` is effects cody
- `contr.poly` is orthogonal polynomial contrasts for **ordinal** factors (not covered)

## Exline Type III `car` Code

```{r}
#| echo: true
options(contrasts = c(unordered = "contr.sum", ordered = "contr.poly"))
library(car)

a_t3 <- aov(vengefulness ~ condition * gender, dat)
Anova(a_t3, type = 3)

```

## Exline Type III `ez`

For Type II and III we can use `car::Anova()` or `ez::ezANOVA()`. For Type III using ``ez::ezANOVA()`, it will handle the contrasts correctly for us on it's own:

```{r}
#| echo: true

library(ez)
ezANOVA(exline, dv = vengefulness, wid = ID, between = c(gender, condition), 
        type = 3)$ANOVA

```

## Output Differences

Note that the interaction **never changes**. Only the main effects results differ for the different types. In this case, the main effects barely even changed! Why?

- [Hint: Does the `ges` column ($\eta^2$) in the `ezANOVA()` output indicate a small or large interaction effect?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [It's a very small interaction effect, so even if we use Type II, The interaction can't really impact the main effects]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

## APA Writeup

The interaction effect is not statistically significant ($F(1, 131) = .02, p = .89$). There is a significant main effect of gender ($F(1, 131) = 4.51$, $p = .04$), but no main effect of condition ($F(1, 131) = .08, p = .77$). Males have higher vengefulness scores than females (Cohen's $d$ = .39).


**Note from Mark (not part of APA writeup):** Post-hoc tests are not necessary for the effect of gender because this variable has only two levels. Means we don't need additional tests and can just calculate $d$ for difference between males and females
